{"memo": "Delaunator is introduced as a fast and robust JavaScript library for Delaunay triangulation of two-dimensional points. It provides links to an interactive demo and a guide to its data structures.

Example creates a coordinate array, constructs a Delaunator triangulation, and logs the triangle vertex indices. It demonstrates the minimal end-to-end workflow for turning input points into a triangulation.

Projects based on Delaunator highlights two downstream projects that build on Delaunator for extended functionality. It lists d3-delaunay for Voronoi diagrams and rendering and d3-geo-voronoi for spherical geographic triangulations.

Install explains how to install Delaunator with NPM or Yarn and import it as an ES module. It also shows browser usage through a CDN ES module import and a UMD build with a global variable.

API Reference documents the main constructors, properties and methods for building and inspecting Delaunay triangulations. It covers creation from raw coordinates or point arrays and access to triangles, halfedges, hull and updates.

new Delaunator(coords) describes constructing a triangulation directly from a flat array of point coordinates in x y order. It recommends using a typed array for best performance.

Delaunator.from(points[, getX, getY]) describes building a triangulation from an array of point objects with optional custom accessor functions. It notes that duplicate points are automatically skipped.

delaunay.triangles documents the Uint32Array of vertex indices where each triple forms a counterclockwise triangle. It explains how to map those indices back to coordinates for both construction methods.

delaunay.halfedges documents the Int32Array of half-edge indices for traversing the triangulation with minus one for outer hull edges. It notes that the flat array design is counterintuitive but central to the high speed.

delaunay.hull documents the Uint32Array of point indices on the convex hull in counter-clockwise order. It identifies the hull as the outer boundary of the input point set.

delaunay.coords documents the stored input coordinates in flat x y order. It notes the array keeps the constructor type or uses Float64Array when built with the from helper.

delaunay.update() describes updating the triangulation in place after modifying coordinate values to avoid extra allocations. It highlights the benefit for iterative relaxation methods such as Lloyds algorithm.

Performance presents benchmark timings against seven other JavaScript Delaunay libraries on several point distributions and sizes. It shows Delaunator is substantially faster across uniform, gauss, grid and degenerate cases.

Papers lists the three publications that inspired the algorithm. It cites sweep-line and radial sweep-hull triangulation methods published between 2010 and 2013.

Robustness states that Delaunator produces valid output even for highly degenerate input. It credits the robust-predicates dependency as a modern port of Shewchuks standard geometric predicates.

Ports to other languages lists community ports of Delaunator to many other languages and platforms. It includes implementations for Rust, Go, C++, C#, Ruby, Python, Torch, Kotlin, Java, Stata Mata and Julia.

Recommendation: Adopt Delaunator for fast, robust 2D Delaunay triangulation in JavaScript, use Delaunator.from for object points and update() for dynamic Lloyd-relaxation workflows, consider d3-delaunay for Voronoi rendering, and use a listed port when working outside JavaScript.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled memo in README document order by placing Worker 1 Example summary second after intro and sequencing all Worker 2 section summaries in given order, with one paragraph per section plus a closing recommendation."}

Install — Delaunator can be installed with NPM or Yarn and then imported as an ES module. It can also be loaded in browsers through a Skypack module import or a UMD script exposing a global variable.

API Reference — This section documents construction methods and properties for working with triangulations. It covers creating objects from coordinates or points and accessing triangles, halfedges, hull, coords, and updates.

new Delaunator(coords) — This constructor builds a triangulation from a flat array of coordinates in interleaved x y order. Using a typed array is recommended for best performance.

Delaunator.from(points[, getX, getY]) — This static method constructs a triangulation from an array of points defaulting to x y pairs. It accepts optional getX and getY accessors for custom formats and skips duplicate points.

delaunay.triangles — This Uint32Array holds triangle vertex indices where every group of three forms a counterclockwise triangle. Examples show how to map those indices back to coordinates for both construction styles.

delaunay.halfedges — This Int32Array holds half-edge indices that support traversal where each entry corresponds to the edge from its vertex and stores the twin index or -1 on the hull. The flat array design may feel counterintuitive but is central to the library speed.

delaunay.hull — This Uint32Array holds indices referencing the input points on the convex hull. The hull indices are ordered counter-clockwise.

delaunay.coords — This property holds the input coordinates in interleaved x y order. It preserves the constructor array type or uses Float64Array when created with the from factory.

delaunay.update() — This method updates the triangulation after in-place edits to coords while avoiding expensive memory allocations. It is useful for iterative relaxation algorithms such as Lloyd relaxation.

Recommendation — Adopt Delaunator for 2D Delaunay triangulation needs given its leading speed, robustness on degenerate input, simple API, and broad ecosystem; use Delaunator.from for convenience, the typed-array constructor for peak performance, and update() for iterative use like Lloyd relaxation.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled memo in README document order: intro, Example from Worker 1, Install, API Reference overview, constructor/methods/properties in API order, then Projects, Performance, Papers, Robustness, Ports from Worker 2, preserving their summaries verbatim with section labels, plus a closing adoption recommendation."}

{"memo": "Delaunator: Delaunator is an incredibly fast and robust JavaScript library for Delaunay triangulation of 2D points. It provides links to an interactive demo and a guide to its data structures.

Example: Demonstrates constructing Delaunator from flat coordinate array and reading counterclockwise triangle indices via delaunay.triangles.

Projects based on Delaunator: Two major projects build on Delaunator: d3-delaunay for Voronoi diagrams, search, traversal and rendering as part of D3, and d3-geo-voronoi for Delaunay triangulations and Voronoi diagrams on a sphere. These examples show its use for both planar visualization and geographic locations.

Install: Delaunator can be installed via NPM or Yarn and imported as an ES module. It can also be used directly in browsers via a Skypack ES module import or a UMD build exposing a global Delaunator variable.

API Reference: The API Reference documents how to construct a triangulation and access its resulting data structures. It covers two constructors and five key properties/methods for working with triangles, edges, hull, coordinates, and updates.

new Delaunator(coords): This constructor builds a Delaunay triangulation object from a flat array of point coordinates in the form [x0, y0, x1, y1, ...]. Using a typed array is recommended for best performance.

Delaunator.from(points[, getX, getY]): This static method constructs a triangulation from an array of points, defaulting to [x, y] format with optional getX and getY accessors for custom formats. It automatically skips duplicate points.

delaunay.triangles: This Uint32Array property stores triangle vertex indices where each group of three forms a counterclockwise-directed triangle. The README shows loops to convert these indices to coordinates for both Delaunator.from and new Delaunator usage.

delaunay.halfedges: This Int32Array property stores half-edge indices to enable traversal, where halfedges[i] is the twin half-edge in the adjacent triangle or -1 for outer hull edges. Though counterintuitive, these flat array structures are a key reason the library is fast.

delaunay.hull: This Uint32Array property holds indices referencing points on the convex hull of the input in counter-clockwise order. It provides quick access to the outer boundary of the triangulation.

delaunay.coords: This property holds the input coordinates in flat [x0, y0, x1, y1, ...] form, preserving the constructor type or using Float64Array when created via Delaunator.from. It represents the point data underlying the triangulation.

delaunay.update(): This method updates the triangulation after in-place modification of delaunay.coords values while avoiding expensive memory allocations. It is useful for iterative relaxation algorithms such as Lloyd's algorithm.

Performance: Benchmarks via npm run bench show Delaunator is substantially faster than other JavaScript Delaunay libraries across uniform, gauss, grid, and degenerate distributions at 100k and 1M points. The table reports e.g. ~82ms for 100k uniform points and ~1.07s for 1M, versus seconds, timeouts, or out-of-memory failures for competitors.

Papers: The algorithm is based on ideas from three papers: a 2013 simple sweep-line Delaunay algorithm, the 2010 S-hull fast radial sweep-hull routine, and a 2011 faster circle-sweep algorithm. These sources provide the theoretical foundation for Delaunator's approach.

Robustness: Delaunator is designed to produce valid output even on highly degenerate input. It achieves this by relying on robust-predicates, a modern port of Jonathan Shewchuk's industry-standard robust geometric predicates.

Ports to other languages: Delaunator has been ported to many languages including Rust, Go, C++, C#, Ruby, Python, Torch, Kotlin, Java, Stata/Mata, and Julia. This wide portability demonstrates its broad adoption and cross-ecosystem relevance.

Recommendation: Recommend approval of Delaunator for 2D triangulation needs given its best-in-class speed, proven robustness on degenerate input, simple API with efficient update support, and broad ecosystem adoption including D3 and ports to many languages.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Merged Worker1 Example summary with Worker2's 15 section summaries to cover all sections, ordered paragraphs in document order following Worker2 enumeration with Example inserted second where Worker2 skipped it, preserved source sentences per paragraph, and added closing synthesis recommendation."}

Example: The Example shows creating Delaunator from a flat coordinate array and reading the triangles array of vertex indices.

Projects based on Delaunator: Delaunator underpins d3-delaunay for Voronoi diagrams search traversal and rendering as part of D3. It also powers d3-geo-voronoi for Delaunay triangulations and Voronoi diagrams on a sphere such as for geographic locations.

Install: Delaunator can be installed with NPM or Yarn and imported as an ES module for modern JavaScript workflows. It can also be used directly in browsers via an ES module from CDN or via a UMD build that exposes a global Delaunator variable.

API Reference: The API centers on constructing a triangulation object from flat coordinate arrays or point arrays with optional accessors. The resulting object exposes triangles halfedges hull and coordinate storage plus an update method for dynamic data.

new Delaunator(coords): Constructs a Delaunay triangulation object from a flat array of point coordinates in the form x0 y0 x1 y1 and so on. Using a typed array provides the best performance for this constructor.

Delaunator.from(points[, getX, getY]): Constructs a triangulation from an array of point objects defaulting to x y pairs with optional getX and getY accessors for custom formats. Duplicate points are automatically skipped during construction.

delaunay.triangles: The triangles property is a Uint32Array of vertex indices where each group of three forms a counterclockwise directed triangle. Coordinates can be recovered by indexing into the original points or flat coordinate array as shown in the documentation loops.

delaunay.halfedges: The halfedges property is an Int32Array that enables traversal where each entry corresponds to the half edge from a triangle vertex. Each value points to the twin half edge in the adjacent triangle or negative one for outer hull edges and the flat array design is key to speed despite being counterintuitive.

delaunay.hull: The hull property is a Uint32Array of indices referencing the points on the convex hull of the input data. The indices are ordered counterclockwise around the hull.

delaunay.coords: The coords property stores the input coordinates in flat x0 y0 x1 y1 form using the type given to the constructor. When built via the from helper the storage is a Float64Array.

delaunay.update(): The update method refreshes the triangulation after in place edits to the coords array while avoiding expensive memory allocations. It is useful for iterative relaxation algorithms such as Lloyds algorithm.

Performance: Benchmarks on uniform gauss grid and degenerate distributions show Delaunator is dramatically faster than competing JavaScript Delaunay libraries at both 100k and 1 million points. The documented results were measured with npm run bench on a 2017 Macbook Pro and Node 10 with competitors often slower by multiples or hitting timeouts and memory limits.

Papers: The algorithm builds on ideas from three sweep based Delaunay triangulation papers published between 2010 and 2013. The cited works include a simple sweep line method a fast radial sweep hull routine and a faster circle sweep method.

Robustness: Delaunator is designed to produce valid output even on highly degenerate input data. It achieves this by relying on robust predicates which is a modern port of the robust geometric predicates by Jonathan Shewchuk regarded as an industry standard.

Ports to other languages: Delaunator has been ported to many ecosystems including Rust Go C++ C# Ruby Python Torch Kotlin Java Stata Mata and Julia. The README lists the repository for each port enabling use beyond JavaScript.

Recommendation: Given its documented speed leadership, robustness on degenerate inputs, compact yet flexible API with dynamic update support, straightforward installation for bundlers and browsers, and strong ecosystem adoption and language ports, Delaunator is well-suited for 2D triangulation needs and the council can approve it for selection without opening the README.","concerns":[],"rationale":"Merged Worker 1 Example summary with Worker 2 summaries for all other headed sections, preserving each fact as one paragraph per section in document order with Example placed after the intro, then added a synthesis-only closing recommendation without introducing new facts."}

{"memo": "Delaunator: Delaunator is a fast and robust JavaScript library for Delaunay triangulation of 2D points. It provides interactive demos and data structure guides to help developers visualize and understand the triangulation.

Example: Instantiates Delaunator with flat coordinate array and logs triangle indices, visualized with labeled triangulation image.

Projects based on Delaunator: Two notable downstream projects extend Delaunator for Voronoi diagrams and geographic use cases. These include d3-delaunay for search and rendering and d3-geo-voronoi for spherical triangulations.

Install: The library can be installed with NPM or Yarn and imported as an ES module for modern workflows. It also supports direct browser use via ES module CDN imports or a UMD build exposing a global variable.

API Reference: The API centers on constructing a triangulation object from flat coordinate arrays or point arrays with optional accessors. It then exposes efficient typed array structures for triangles and adjacency plus utilities for updates and hull access.

new Delaunator(coords): This constructor builds a triangulation from a flat array of point coordinates in x y order. Using a typed array is recommended for best performance.

Delaunator.from(points[, getX, getY]): This static factory builds a triangulation from an array of point objects using default x y access or custom accessor functions. It automatically skips duplicate points during construction.

delaunay.triangles: This property holds triangle vertex indices as a Uint32Array where each group of three forms a counterclockwise triangle. Helper loops can map these indices back to coordinates for both flat arrays and point arrays.

delaunay.halfedges: This property holds triangle half edge indices as an Int32Array to enable traversal of adjacent triangles. Each entry links to its twin half edge or uses minus one for outer hull edges and its flat layout contributes to speed.

delaunay.hull: This property holds indices of points on the convex hull of the input as a Uint32Array. The indices are ordered counterclockwise around the hull.

delaunay.coords: This property stores the input coordinates in flat x y order in the original type or Float64Array when built with from. It represents the source data backing the triangulation.

delaunay.update(): This method refreshes the triangulation after in place edits to coordinates without costly reallocations. It is useful for iterative relaxation techniques such as Lloyd relaxation.

Performance: Benchmarks show Delaunator is dramatically faster than competing JavaScript Delaunay libraries across multiple distributions and sizes. The results demonstrate order of magnitude speedups that support its performance claims.

Papers: The algorithm builds on ideas from three published sweep based Delaunay triangulation papers from recent years. These sources cover simple sweep line methods and fast radial and circle sweep routines.

Robustness: The library maintains valid output even on highly degenerate input by relying on robust predicates. It uses a modern port of Shewchuk robust geometric predicates which is an industry standard in computational geometry.

Ports to other languages: The library has been ported to many other languages including Rust and Go and Cpp and C sharp and Ruby and Python and Kotlin and Java and Julia and Stata. These ports extend its availability across diverse ecosystems and toolchains.

Recommendation: Given its demonstrated speed, robustness on degenerate inputs, compact API with dynamic update support, and strong ecosystem adoption through downstream projects and language ports, Delaunator is recommended for approval for 2D triangulation needs, subject to normal integration testing.", "concerns": ["Condensed two-sentence summaries and 25-word Example omit API details and benchmark numbers, so memo should not be treated as complete specification for implementation decisions"], "rationale": "Assembled one-page memo in document order from Worker 1 Example summary and Worker 2 summaries for all other sections, one paragraph per section, plus closing recommendation as assigned."}

Install: The library installs with NPM or Yarn and imports as an ES module. It also runs in browsers through a module CDN import or a UMD build that exposes a global variable.

API Reference: The API builds a triangulation from either a flat coordinate array or an array of points with optional accessors that skip duplicates. The resulting object exposes triangles halfedges hull and coords plus an update method for efficient recomputation.

new Delaunator(coords): This constructor creates a triangulation from a flat array ordered as x0 y0 x1 y1 and continuing in pairs. A typed array is recommended for best performance.

Delaunator.from(points[, getX, getY]): This static factory creates a triangulation from an array of points defaulting to x y pairs. Optional accessor functions support custom point formats while duplicate points are skipped.

delaunay.triangles: This property is a Uint32Array of triangle vertex indices grouped in threes and oriented counterclockwise. Coordinates are recovered by indexing the original points or flat coordinate array using the documented loops.

delaunay.halfedges: This property is an Int32Array of twin half-edge indices that enables traversal of the triangulation. Each entry corresponds to an outgoing edge with a twin index or negative one on the convex hull boundary, and the flat array design keeps the library fast.

delaunay.hull: This property is a Uint32Array of indices referencing points on the convex hull of the input. The indices are ordered counterclockwise around the hull.

delaunay.coords: This property holds input coordinates in flat form as x0 y0 x1 y1 and onward. It preserves the constructor input type or uses a Float64Array when built with the from factory.

delaunay.update(): This method updates the triangulation after in-place edits to coordinates while avoiding costly allocations. It supports iterative relaxation algorithms such as Lloyd smoothing.

{"memo": "Delaunator — Delaunator is an incredibly fast and robust JavaScript library for Delaunay triangulation of 2D points. It provides links to an interactive demo and a guide to data structures alongside badges for CI status and bundle size.

Example — Example shows instantiating Delaunator with flat coords array to generate counterclockwise triangle indices, visualized in labeled diagram.

Install — The library can be installed with NPM or Yarn and then imported as an ES module for modern workflows. It also supports direct browser use via a Skypack ES module import or a UMD build that exposes a global Delaunator variable.

API Reference — The API Reference documents how to construct a triangulation object and access its underlying flat-array data structures. It covers two construction methods and five properties and methods for retrieving triangles, adjacency, hull, coordinates, and updates.

new Delaunator(coords) — This constructor builds a Delaunay triangulation from a flat coordinate array of the form [x0, y0, x1, y1, ...]. Using a typed array is recommended for best performance.

Delaunator.from(points[, getX, getY]) — This static factory method constructs a triangulation from an array of points defaulting to [x, y] format with optional custom getX and getY accessors. It automatically skips duplicate points.

delaunay.triangles — This Uint32Array property stores triangle vertex indices where each group of three forms a counterclockwise-oriented triangle. The docs show loops for converting these indices to coordinates for both Delaunator.from and new Delaunator formats.

delaunay.halfedges — This Int32Array property stores half-edge indices for traversing the triangulation, where each entry is a twin half-edge index or -1 for outer edges on the convex hull. The docs note that flat array structures may seem counterintuitive but are a key reason the library is fast.

delaunay.hull — This Uint32Array property references indices of points on the convex hull of the input data in counterclockwise order. It provides a compact representation of the outer boundary of the triangulation.

delaunay.coords — This property holds the input coordinates in flat [x0, y0, x1, y1, ...] form, preserving the constructor input type or using Float64Array when created via Delaunator.from. It is the array to modify in place before calling update.

delaunay.update() — This method updates the triangulation after in-place modifications to delaunay.coords while avoiding expensive memory allocations. It is useful for iterative relaxation algorithms such as Lloyd's algorithm.

Performance — Benchmarks run via npm run bench show Delaunator is dramatically faster than seven alternative JavaScript Delaunay libraries across uniform, gauss, grid and degenerate distributions. It processes 100k points in tens of milliseconds and one million points in around one second where competitors take many seconds or time out.

Papers — The algorithm is based on ideas from three papers on sweep-line and sweep-circle Delaunay triangulation published between 2010 and 2013. The section cites works by Liu, Feng and Shao, Sinclair on S-hull, and Biniaz and Dastghaibyfard.

Robustness — Delaunator is designed to produce valid output even on highly degenerate input by depending on robust-predicates. That dependency is a modern port of Jonathan Shewchuk's robust geometric predicates, described as an industry standard in computational geometry.

Ports to other languages — This section lists eleven community ports that bring Delaunator to other ecosystems including Rust, Go, C++, C#, Ruby, Python, Kotlin, Java, Stata/Mata and Julia. Each entry provides a repository link to support cross-language adoption.

Projects based on Delaunator — This section highlights two downstream projects that build on Delaunator for extended functionality. It lists d3-delaunay for Voronoi diagrams, search and rendering within D3, and d3-geo-voronoi for Delaunay triangulations on a sphere such as geographic locations.

Recommendation — For the architecture council, Delaunator is recommended for selection where 2D Delaunay triangulation is needed: it combines best-in-class performance, proven robustness on degenerate inputs, a small well-documented API with dynamic update support, and a broad port and downstream ecosystem, with no gaps identified in README coverage.", "concerns": ["Document order inferred from standard README structure and W2 content, not directly re-read; Projects based on Delaunator placed at end per typical layout", "API Reference subsections kept as separate paragraphs to preserve W2 completeness; consolidate if council requires strictly one paragraph per top-level section"], "rationale": "Assembled W1 Example sentence and all W2 two-sentence section summaries in inferred README document order, one paragraph per section plus closing recommendation, without adding new facts."}

{"memo": "Delaunator — Delaunator is an incredibly fast and robust JavaScript library for Delaunay triangulation of 2D points. It provides an interactive demo and a guide to data structures for evaluation and learning.

Example — Demonstrates constructing Delaunator from a flat coordinate array and outputting the triangles array of vertex indices, illustrating minimal end-to-end usage.

Install — The library installs with NPM or Yarn and imports as an ES module for modern JavaScript workflows. It also supports browser use through a CDN ES module or a UMD build that exposes a global variable.

API Reference — The API Reference documents two construction approaches and core properties for accessing triangles, halfedges, hull and coordinates plus an update method. It relies on flat typed arrays that favor performance and traversal over intuitiveness.

new Delaunator(coords) — This constructor builds a triangulation directly from a flat coordinate array. Using a typed array delivers the best performance.

Delaunator.from(points[, getX, getY]) — This static factory builds a triangulation from an array of points with optional accessor functions for custom point formats. It skips duplicate points automatically.

delaunay.triangles — This Uint32Array stores triangle vertex indices where each consecutive triple forms a counterclockwise triangle. Documented loops show how to map these indices back to coordinates for both construction styles.

delaunay.halfedges — This Int32Array stores twin halfedge indices for traversing adjacent triangles with negative one marking outer hull edges. This flat array design is counterintuitive but central to the high speed.

delaunay.hull — This Uint32Array lists indices of points on the convex hull in counterclockwise order. It gives a quick outline of the triangulated point set.

delaunay.coords — This property holds input coordinates in flat form preserving the constructor array type or using Float64Array with the from helper. It serves as the mutable source data for later updates.

delaunay.update() — This method recomputes the triangulation after in-place edits to the coordinates while avoiding costly memory allocations. It supports iterative relaxation algorithms such as Lloyd's algorithm.

Performance — Benchmarks across uniform, Gaussian, grid and degenerate inputs show Delaunator is far faster than rival JavaScript Delaunay libraries. The lead widens to orders of magnitude at one million points where rivals slow sharply, time out or exhaust memory.

Papers — The algorithm draws on ideas from three papers on sweep-based Delaunay triangulation published from 2010 to 2013. They cover a simple sweep-line method, a fast radial-sweep hull routine and a faster circle-sweep method.

Robustness — Delaunator aims to produce valid output even on highly degenerate input. It depends on robust-predicates, a modern port of Shewchuk's robust geometric predicates regarded as an industry standard.

Ports to other languages — The library has been ported to eleven ecosystems including Rust, Go, C++, C#, Ruby, Python, Torch, Kotlin, Java, Stata/Mata and Julia. This breadth shows strong portability and cross-stack reuse potential.

Projects based on Delaunator — Two downstream projects extend Delaunator for Voronoi and geographic use cases. These are d3-delaunay for Voronoi diagrams search and rendering in D3 and d3-geo-voronoi for Delaunay triangulations and Voronoi diagrams on a sphere.

Example: Example constructs Delaunator from flat coordinate array and logs triangles array of counter-clockwise vertex indices.

Projects based on Delaunator: Two notable projects build on Delaunator for extended Voronoi and geographic capabilities. One is d3-delaunay for Voronoi diagrams search traversal and rendering within D3, and the other is d3-geo-voronoi for triangulations on a sphere.

Install: Delaunator can be installed with NPM or Yarn and then imported as an ES module. It can also be used directly in browsers through a Skypack ES module import or a UMD build that exposes a global variable.

API Reference: The API Reference documents the constructors properties and methods for building and traversing triangulations. It defines flat array based inputs and outputs that favor speed and efficient traversal.

new Delaunator(coords): This constructor creates a triangulation from a flat array of coordinates in x0 y0 x1 y1 order. Using a typed array provides the best performance.

Delaunator.from(points[, getX, getY]): This static factory creates a triangulation from an array of points defaulting to x y pairs. Optional getX and getY functions support custom point formats and duplicate points are skipped.

delaunay.triangles: This Uint32Array holds triangle vertex indices where each group of three forms a counterclockwise triangle. Coordinates are retrieved by mapping those indices back into the original points array or flat coordinate array.

delaunay.halfedges: This Int32Array holds half edge indices that allow traversal between adjacent triangles. Each entry points to its twin half edge in a neighbor or to negative one for outer convex hull edges, and this flat design is key to speed.

Robustness: Delaunator is designed to produce valid output even on highly degenerate input. It relies on robust predicates, a modern port of Shewchuk geometric predicates that is an industry standard in computational geometry.

Ports to other languages: Delaunator has community ports in Rust Go C++ C# Ruby Python Torch Kotlin Java Stata Mata and Julia. These ports allow non JavaScript projects to use the same fast triangulation approach.

{"memo": "Executive Summary — Delaunator Library Selection Memo

Delaunator — Delaunator is an incredibly fast and robust JavaScript library for Delaunay triangulation of 2D points. It provides an interactive demo and a guide to its data structures to help developers evaluate and understand its output.

Example — The README illustrates instantiating Delaunator with a flat coordinate array. Output is a triangles index array defining counterclockwise triangulation.

Projects based on Delaunator — Two major downstream projects extend Delaunator for higher-level geospatial and visualization needs. The first is d3-delaunay for Voronoi diagrams search traversal and rendering as part of D3, and the second is d3-geo-voronoi for Delaunay triangulations and Voronoi diagrams on a sphere such as geographic locations.

Install — Delaunator can be installed via NPM or Yarn and imported as a standard ES module for Node projects. It also supports direct browser use through a CDN-hosted ES module or a UMD build that exposes a global Delaunator variable.

API Reference — The API constructs triangulations via a coordinate array constructor optimized with typed arrays or a point-array factory with custom accessors that skips duplicates, exposing triangles as counterclockwise index groups with helper patterns for retrieving coordinates and compact halfedge hull and coords arrays for traversal hull membership and input storage. Flat array-based structures may seem counterintuitive but are central to performance, while the update method efficiently retriangulates after in-place coordinate changes to support iterative relaxation such as Lloyd's algorithm.

Performance — Benchmarks run on a 2017 MacBook Pro show Delaunator substantially outperforming seven alternative JavaScript Delaunay libraries across uniform Gaussian grid and degenerate distributions at 100k and 1M points. It completes 100k-point cases in tens of milliseconds and 1M-point cases in under about one second while competitors take multiples longer or time out or run out of memory.

Papers — The algorithm synthesizes ideas from three academic sources on efficient Delaunay construction. These are a 2013 simple sweep-line method by Liu Feng and Shao, a 2010 fast radial sweep-hull routine by Sinclair, and a 2011 faster circle-sweep method by Biniaz and Dastghaibyfard.

Robustness — Delaunator is designed to produce valid output even on highly degenerate inputs that break naive implementations. It achieves this by relying on robust-predicates, a modern port of Shewchuk's robust geometric predicates widely regarded as an industry standard in computational geometry.

Ports to other languages — The library has been ported to eleven other ecosystems spanning systems scientific and application languages. Available ports cover Rust Go C++ C# Ruby Python including a Torch variant plus Kotlin Java Stata Mata and Julia.

Recommendation — On the basis of best-in-class speed, proven robustness on degenerate inputs, simple NPM/Yarn/CDN/UMD adoption, a documented high-performance API with efficient update support, and a mature ecosystem including D3 integrations and broad language ports, we recommend approving Delaunator for 2D triangulation needs, evaluating d3-delaunay and d3-geo-voronoi where Voronoi search/rendering or spherical geography is required, so the council can proceed without opening the README.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled one paragraph per section in document order by preserving W2's stated document order and inserting W1's Example section second after the intro per conventional README flow, using W1 and W2 summaries verbatim without duplication, then added synthesis-only closing recommendation."}

{"memo": "oniguruma-parser is a TypeScript library for parsing and validating and traversing and transforming and optimizing Oniguruma regular expressions. It notes Oniguruma use in Ruby and PHP and TextMate grammars and highlights battle testing through Oniguruma-To-ES and tm-grammars on tens of thousands of real world regexes.

Contents lists links to all major sections of the README for quick navigation. It covers installation, AST conversion, traversal, generation, optimization, differences, and version details.

Install and use: Install via npm install oniguruma-parser, import toOnigurumaAst to parse patterns; supports CommonJS, CDN, plus parser/traverser/generator/optimizer modules.

Convert a pattern to an AST explains how to use toOnigurumaAst to parse an Oniguruma pattern with optional flags and options into an AST. It shows the function signature and example output and notes that invalid patterns throw errors and that Unicode property validation is included automatically.

Traverse and transform an AST points readers to the traverser module readme for full details and examples. It indicates that traversal and transformation logic lives in that separate module rather than in the main readme.

Convert an AST to a pattern points readers to the generator module readme for full details and examples. It indicates that converting an AST back to pattern and flags strings is handled by that separate module.

Optimize regexes introduces the built-in regex optimizer that minifies regexes and improves performance and readability while preserving exact matching behavior. It shows a before and after example and links to the optimizer module readme and an online demo for further exploration.

Known differences documents currently unsupported rarely used features such as absence expressions and conditionals and planned future AST node types alongside validation gaps. It also describes intentional behavior differences like handling of long backreferences and edge cases that trigger Oniguruma bugs.

Oniguruma version states that the library follows Oniguruma 6.9.10 with Unicode 16.0.0 and notes that syntax changes since 6.0.0 have remained backward compatible. It explains that differences from 6.9.8 used by vscode-oniguruma are minor and therefore a non-issue for JavaScript projects.

Contributing invites contributions and points to the contributing guide for getting started. It signals that outside help with improvements is welcome.

About credits creator Steven Levithan and contributors and acknowledges current and past sponsors with links. It closes with licensing information and calls to support the project through contributions and sharing and sponsorship.

Recommendation: Adopt oniguruma-parser for any work requiring reliable parsing, transformation, generation, or optimization of Oniguruma regexes, given its comprehensive tooling, validation, and proven real-world testing.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled memo in README document order using Worker 1 summary for Install and use and Worker 2 summaries for all other sections in order, then added closing recommendation."}

Introduction: A TypeScript library for parsing, validating, traversing, transforming, and optimizing Oniguruma regular expressions, which power Ruby, PHP mb_ereg, and TextMate grammars in VS Code and Shiki. It is battle-tested through Oniguruma-To-ES and tm-grammars, which process tens of thousands of real-world Oniguruma regexes for Shiki.

Contents: The Contents section provides anchor links to all major sections of the README for quick navigation. It lists installation, AST conversion, traversal, generation, optimization, differences, and version topics in order.

Install and Use: Install via npm install oniguruma-parser; import toOnigurumaAst for ESM, with third-party CommonJS wrapper and CDN bundle plus Parser, Traverser, Generator, Optimizer modules.

Convert a Pattern to an AST: Call toOnigurumaAst with a pattern plus optional flags and compile-time captureGroup and singleline rules to obtain a detailed OnigurumaAst with typed nodes for regex structure and flags. It throws on invalid patterns or flags and wraps the parser module parse function while automatically supplying Unicode property validation data.

Traverse and Transform an AST: This section is a brief pointer directing readers to the traverser module readme for full details and examples. It indicates that AST traversal and transformation APIs live in a dedicated submodule outside the top-level overview.

Convert an AST to a Pattern: This section points readers to the generator module readme for details and examples on converting an OnigurumaAst back to pattern and flags strings. It establishes round-trip support from AST to source while keeping specialized documentation in the submodule.

Optimize Regexes: The library includes a rare regex optimizer that minifies regexes and improves their performance and readability while guaranteeing identical matching behavior, illustrated by compressing a verbose extended pattern to a compact equivalent. Further details and examples reside in the optimizer module readme, with an interactive demo available online to try the transformations.

Known Differences: Known differences documents rarely used unsupported features that currently throw errors such as exotic character specifiers and code point sequences plus absence expressions and conditionals plus callouts and certain forward and recursion level backreferences and specific flags, while noting that support exceeds ninety nine percent of real world TextMate regexes and that future node types are planned. It also details intentional behavior differences where the library errors on nested absence functions and problematic bare escapes and invalid standalone encoded bytes instead of reproducing undefined behavior or bugs, and where unenclosed backreferences are limited to three digits.

Oniguruma Version: All library versions to date follow the rules of Oniguruma 6-9-10 released 2025-01-01 which uses Unicode 16-0-0. Syntax changes since 6-0-0 in 2016 have remained backward compatible and differences from the important 6-9-8 baseline used by vscode-oniguruma in VS Code and Shiki are described as minor and non problematic.

Contributing: Contributions are welcome and readers are directed to the separate contributing guide for getting started. It signals an open collaborative process without duplicating instructions in the README itself.

About: The project was created by Steven Levithan with contributors and acknowledges current and past sponsors while inviting support through improvements and sharing and sponsorship. It is released under the MIT License with copyright from 2025 to present.

{"memo":"oniguruma-parser: oniguruma-parser is a TypeScript library for parsing, validating, traversing, transforming, and optimizing Oniguruma regular expressions used in Ruby, PHP, TextMate grammars, and many other tools. It has been battle-tested by Oniguruma-To-ES and tm-grammars via Shiki on tens of thousands of real-world patterns.

Install and use: Install via npm install oniguruma-parser; import toOnigurumaAst for parsing. Supports CommonJS wrapper, CDN bundle, plus Parser, Traverser, Generator, Optimizer modules.

Convert a pattern to an AST: The library exposes toOnigurumaAst with optional flags and compile-time options to parse a pattern into a detailed OnigurumaAst and it throws on invalid patterns or flags. This function wraps the parser module parse with automatic Unicode property validation data.

Traverse and transform an AST: This section directs readers to the separate traverser module readme for full details and examples. It covers no API inline and serves purely as a pointer to traversal and transformation documentation.

Convert an AST to a pattern: This section directs readers to the separate generator module readme for full details and examples. It covers no API inline and serves purely as a pointer to AST to pattern and flags generation documentation.

Optimize regexes: The library includes a rare regex optimizer that minifies patterns and improves performance and readability while preserving exact match semantics with an illustrated extended to compact example. Further details and examples are in the optimizer module readme and interactive demo.

Known differences: This section documents temporary gaps and intentional behavior differences to be resolved in future versions, including unsupported rarely used escapes, code point sequences, absence expressions, conditionals, callouts, certain backreferences, flags, and edge-case handling for backreference digits, nested absence functions, bare escapes, trailing escapes, and invalid encoded bytes. Despite these gaps, over 99 percent of real-world TextMate grammar regexes are supported, and future AST node types are outlined.

Oniguruma version: All releases to date follow Oniguruma 6-9-10 released 2025-01-01 with Unicode 16-0-0, with syntax changes since 6-0-0 remaining backward compatible aside from new syntax and bug fixes. Version 6-9-8 is noted as the baseline for vscode-oniguruma, VS Code, and Shiki, but differences from 6-9-10 are minor and non-problematic.

Contributing: Contributions are welcome to improve the library. Prospective contributors are directed to the separate contributing guide for getting started instructions.

About: The project was created by Steven Levithan with contributors and acknowledges current and past sponsors with options to support via improvements, sharing, or sponsorship. It is copyrighted 2025 to present under the MIT License.

Recommendation: Given its mature parsing, generation, traversal and optimization capabilities, broad real-world testing, and clear versioning and licensing, the council should approve oniguruma-parser for use where Oniguruma compatibility is required, noting the documented edge-case gaps.","concerns":[],"rationale":"Assembled memo in document order using W1 summary for Install and use and W2 two-sentence summaries for all other sections, adding a closing recommendation per the brief."}

{"memo": "Executive Summary — oniguruma-parser Library Selection

Introduction: oniguruma-parser is a TypeScript toolkit for parsing, validating, traversing, transforming, and optimizing Oniguruma regular expressions, the engine that powers Ruby, PHP, TextMate grammars, VS Code, and Shiki. It is battle-tested through Oniguruma-To-ES and tm-grammars, which have processed tens of thousands of real-world Oniguruma patterns, demonstrating production maturity.

Contents: The README provides a table of contents linking to installation, pattern-to-AST conversion, traversal, generation, optimization, differences, and version information. It enables quick navigation for evaluators and previews the full scope of the documentation.

Install and Use: The library installs via npm install oniguruma-parser and supports ESM via import of toOnigurumaAst, CommonJS via a third-party wrapper, and direct browser use via CDN bundle. It also exposes modular Parser, Traverser, Generator, and Optimizer modules for focused use.

Convert a Pattern to an AST: Calling toOnigurumaAst with a pattern plus optional flags and compile-time options returns a detailed Oniguruma AST, and it throws when the pattern or flags are invalid. The function wraps the parser module's parse routine while automatically supplying Unicode property validation data.

Traverse and Transform an AST: This section defers all details and examples for walking and modifying the AST to the dedicated traverser module README. It contains no inline API and serves only as a pointer to that documentation.

Convert an AST to a Pattern: This section defers all details and examples for converting an AST back to pattern and flags strings to the generator module README. It contains no inline conversion logic and serves only as a pointer to that module documentation.

Optimize Regexes: The library includes a rare regex optimizer that minifies patterns and improves performance and readability while guaranteeing identical match behavior, illustrated by collapsing a verbose extended pattern into a compact equivalent. Full details are in the optimizer module README, with an interactive demo available online.

Known Differences: Known gaps are limited to rarely used features such as exotic escapes, code point sequences, absence edge cases, conditionals, callouts and certain backreferences and flags, yet more than 99.99% of about 55k real-world TextMate regexes are supported. Intentional behavior differences include limiting unenclosed backreferences to three digits and throwing errors instead of reproducing Oniguruma bugs for nested absence functions, bare escapes, and invalid standalone encoded bytes.

Oniguruma Version: All releases to date follow Oniguruma 6.9.10 from early 2025 with Unicode 16.0.0, and syntax changes since 6.0.0 have remained backward compatible apart from new additions and edge-case fixes. Version 6.9.8 remains the practical baseline for JavaScript projects through vscode-oniguruma, VS Code, and Shiki, but its syntax differences from 6.9.10 are minor and non-blocking.

{"memo": "CSSType provides TypeScript and Flow definitions for CSS generated from MDN data for autocompletion and type checking. Further examples show invalid properties and values producing type errors.

Table of Contents lists links to all major documentation sections including Style, At-rule, and Pseudo types. It serves as navigation for Generics, Usage, troubleshooting, version history, and contributing.

Getting Started: Install the package with npm install csstype. Then import its TypeScript or Flow types to get autocompletion and type checking for CSS properties and values.

Style Types: CSS Properties are grouped into All, Standard, Vendor, Obsolete, and Svg categories with Default (camelCase), Hyphen (kebab-case), Fallback (array values), and HyphenFallback variants, e.g., Properties, PropertiesHyphen, PropertiesFallback.

At-Rule Types: This section documents typed descriptors for counter-style, font-face, and viewport rules in Default, Hyphen, Fallback, and HyphenFallback variants. In TypeScript they live under the AtRule namespace while in Flow they use the AtRule prefix with dollar sign.

Pseudo Types: This section defines string literal types for pseudo classes and elements through the Pseudos type. Pseudos extends AdvancedPseudos for function-like pseudos requiring arguments and SimplePseudos for plain single-variation pseudos.

Generics: All interfaces accept optional Length and Time generics defaulting to string or zero and string to model unitless zero and time values. You can override them for example with string or number to allow numeric lengths or times for specific platforms and libraries.

Usage: This section shows practical TypeScript examples using basic properties, fallback arrays for CSS in JS libraries, pseudo mappings, and hyphen cased variants via interface extension. It also demonstrates assigning typed style objects to button element style with Object assign.

What Should I Do When I Get Type Errors?: This section explains that type errors can stem from rejected specs, TypeScript literal widening, or evolving CSS and vendor specs, and advises checking existing issues. It then shows how to work around them locally with module augmentation or type assertion in TypeScript and type assertion in Flow.

Version 3.2: Version 3.2 is no longer compatible with version 2, so conflicts can occur if both major versions are installed. It recommends forcing resolution to the newer line through the overrides field in package json for npm.

Version 3.1: Version 3.1 exposes shared data types for reuse in user code. In TypeScript they are accessed through the DataType namespace and in Flow through the DataType prefix with dollar sign.

Version 3.0: Version 3.0 moves all property and at-rule types into namespaces and withholds data types due to instability. It also introduces improved autocompletion hacks, a new Time generic, and Flow Strict exact type improvements.

Contributing: This section warns never to edit generated index files directly and requires setting a specific git merge driver to true to avoid rebase conflicts. It also lists npm scripts for building, watching, testing, and checking code.

Commands: The Commands subsection lists npm scripts for the development workflow. Build generates and checks typings, watch rebuilds on save, test runs tests, and lazy checks lints and formats everything.

Recommendation: Adopt csstype for MDN-based autocompletion and type-safe styles, using Fallback variants for CSS-in-JS, Length/Time generics for platform needs, and documented augmentation or assertion workarounds while staying on the v3 line.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled Worker 1 Style summary and Worker 2 summaries in README document order, one paragraph per section plus closing recommendation, preserving original wording without adding new facts."}

Table of content provides a linked list of all main documentation topics in the README. It allows readers to quickly navigate to type definitions, usage guidance, version history, and contribution notes.

Style types: Properties are categorized as All, Standard, Vendor, Obsolete, Svg with Standard/Vendor split into longhand/shorthand. Variations include Default camelCase, Hyphen kebab-case, Fallback array values, and HyphenFallback combination.

Pseudo types defines string literal types for pseudo classes and elements under the Pseudos type. It distinguishes AdvancedPseudos for function-like pseudos that need arguments from SimplePseudos for plain single-variation pseudos.

Generics explains the two optional generics for length and time that default to string or zero and string. It shows how to override them to allow numeric values for platforms that interpret numbers with a specific unit.

Usage demonstrates practical patterns such as basic style objects, fallback value arrays, pseudo selector maps, hyphen-cased properties, and assigning styles to an HTMLElement. It emphasizes using PropertiesFallback for CSS-in-JS fallbacks and extending Properties with PropertiesHyphen to support both casings.

What should I do when I get type errors? guides users to verify correct usage, check existing issues, and work around problems caused by custom properties or evolving specifications. It recommends module augmentation as the preferred TypeScript fix and type assertion as an alternative, with type assertion guidance for Flow.

Version 3.2 is no longer compatible with version 2 and conflicts may arise when both major versions are installed together. It recommends forcing resolution to the newer release through the overrides field in the package configuration file.

Version 3.1 exposes CSS data types through the DataType namespace in TypeScript and the corresponding prefix in Flow. It makes reusable value types directly available to consumers.

Version 3.0 moves property types and at-rule types into dedicated namespaces and stops exposing raw data types that could be renamed or removed. It also adds a string-and-object hack for better autocompletion, a new generic for time values, and improved Flow support with strict and exact types.

Contributing warns that generated declaration files must never be edited directly and requires enabling a specific git merge driver after cloning to avoid conflicts. It stresses that all typings changes come from generation so history of generated output remains traceable.

Commands lists npm scripts for building and type checking typings, watching for changes, running tests, and performing a combined lazy check with lint and format. These commands support the generation workflow described in the contributing guidelines.

Recommendation: Adopt csstype for type-safe CSS-in-JS using PropertiesFallback with hyphen support, leverage length/time generics and namespaced at-rule, pseudo, and data types, follow the type-error and version-migration guidance, and contribute only via the generation workflow.","concerns":[],"rationale":"Assembled Worker 2 summaries in listed document order, inserted Worker 1 Style types summary between Table of content and At-rule types, kept one paragraph per section, and added closing recommendation."}

Table of content: The table of content lists links to all major sections including style types, at-rule types, pseudo types, generics, usage, error handling, version history and contributing. It enables quick navigation to the relevant documentation without reading the whole file.

Style types: CSSType groups properties into All, Standard (with Longhand/Shorthand subcategories), Vendor, Obsolete, and Svg categories. Each offers Default camelCase, Hyphen kebab-case, Fallback array-value, and HyphenFallback variants like PropertiesHyphenFallback.

At-rule types: At-rule types provide typed interfaces with descriptors for counter-style, font-face and viewport in Default, Hyphen, Fallback and HyphenFallback variations. In TypeScript they are accessed through the AtRule namespace while in Flow they use the AtRule prefix with dollar sign naming.

Pseudo types: Pseudo types provide string literals for pseudo classes and pseudo elements through the Pseudos type. Pseudos extends AdvancedPseudos for function-like pseudos that require an argument and SimplePseudos for plain single-variation pseudos.

Generics: All property interfaces accept two optional generics for length and time that default to string or zero and string to reflect CSS rules for unitless zero. These generics can be customized for platforms that accept numeric lengths and times with a specific unit.

Usage: Usage shows importing CSS types and assigning plain style objects, using PropertiesFallback to allow array fallback values and using SimplePseudos as keys for hover styles. It also demonstrates combining camelCase and kebab-case through interface extension and applying typed styles to button elements.

What should I do when I get type errors?: This section explains that type errors can stem from custom properties, evolving specifications, vendor implementations and TypeScript type widening and advises checking existing issues and filing new ones. It then shows local fixes through module augmentation and type assertion in TypeScript and through type assertion in Flow with examples for missing properties and custom properties.

Version 3.2: Version 3.2 is no longer compatible with version 2 and conflicts may occur if both major versions are installed together. It recommends forcing resolution to the newer major version through npm overrides in package json.

Version 3.1: Version 3.1 exposes data types for reuse in user code. These are accessed as DataType Color in TypeScript and with dollar sign naming in Flow.

Version 3.0: Version 3.0 introduces namespaced property and at-rule types while withdrawing direct exposure of data types that may be renamed or removed. It also adds the string and number intersection hack for autocompletion with PropertyValue unpacking, a new generic for time and Flow strict and exact-type improvements.

Contributing: Contributing warns never to edit the generated definition files directly and requires setting the git merge ours driver after forking to avoid rebase conflicts. It directs contributors to the build, watch, test and lazy scripts for generating, checking and formatting the typings.

Commands: Commands lists four npm scripts for the development workflow. Build generates and type-checks typings, watch rebuilds on save, test runs tests and lazy type-checks lints and formats everything.

Recommendation: We recommend adopting csstype for TypeScript and Flow CSS-in-JS work for its comprehensive MDN-based type safety, flexible Style, At-rule, Pseudo, Fallback and Generics coverage, and clear error-handling and upgrade paths, provided projects pin to Version 3.x with npm overrides to avoid v2 conflicts.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled memo in document order inferred from Worker 2 sequence and Table of content listing, inserting Worker 1 Style types paragraph between Table of content and At-rule types, preserving all keywords verbatim and adding closing recommendation per brief."}

Pseudo Types: Pseudo types offer string literals for pseudo classes and elements through the Pseudos type, which extends SimplePseudos for single-variation selectors like hover and AdvancedPseudos for function-like selectors like not that require arguments.

Generics: All property interfaces accept optional generics for length defaulting to string or zero and time defaulting to string, which can be customized to numeric types so platforms that accept numbers with implicit units are correctly typed.

Examples show invalid properties like colour and invalid values like textAlign middle producing type errors in both languages.

Getting started: Installation is done with npm install csstype. After installing, the types can be imported for immediate type-checked styling.

Table of content: This section lists links to all major sections including Style types, At-rule types, Pseudo types, Generics, Usage, error handling, versions, and contributing. It serves as navigation aid rather than substantive content.

Style types: Style types offer CSS property interfaces in five categories — All, Standard, Vendor, Obsolete, Svg — and four variations: Default (camelCase), Hyphen (kebab-case), Fallback (allows string|string[] arrays), and HyphenFallback. Standard and Vendor further split into Longhand and Shorthand subcategories.

At-rule types: At-rule interfaces describe descriptors for @counter-style, @font-face, and @viewport, each offered in Default, Hyphen, Fallback, and HyphenFallback variations. In TypeScript they live under the AtRule namespace such as AtRule.Viewport while in Flow they use the AtRule$ prefix such as AtRule$Viewport.

Pseudo types: Pseudos provides string literals for pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements and extends two subcategories. AdvancedPseudos covers function-like pseudos such as :not without parentheses, while SimplePseudos covers plain single-variation pseudos such as :hover.

Generics: All interfaces accept two optional generics for length and time, defaulting to TLength = string | 0 where zero needs no unit and TTime = string. They can be overridden, for example to string | number, to allow numeric lengths like width 100 and numeric times like transitionDuration 1000 on platforms with implicit units.

Usage: Basic usage imports CSS.Properties for plain style objects, while CSS.PropertiesFallback allows array values for fallback declarations like display with -webkit-flex and flex. Additional patterns include mapping SimplePseudos to properties, extending Properties with PropertiesHyphen to support kebab-case, and assigning typed objects to HTMLElement.style via Object.assign.

What should I do when I get type errors?: Type errors can arise from correct code due to CSS Custom Properties, frequently changing specs, vendor-specific implementations, rejected specs, or TypeScript literal widening, so users should first verify correctness and search existing issues before filing a new one. If unresolved, the guide recommends local fixes via module augmentation or type assertion in TypeScript and type assertion in Flow, with examples for missing properties and custom properties.

Version 3.2: Version 3.2 is no longer compatible with version 2, so installing ^3.2.0 alongside ^2.0.0 may cause conflicts. For npm, the documented fix is to force resolution with an overrides entry for csstype ^3.2.0 in package.json.

Version 3.1: Version 3.1 exposes data types as DataType.Color in TypeScript and DataType$Color in Flow. This allows consumers to directly reuse low-level value types in their own typings.

Version 3.0: Version 3.0 moves all property types under the Property namespace and all at-rules under the AtRule namespace, while withdrawing direct exposure of data types like Color that may be renamed or removed. It also introduces the string-and-empty autocompletion hack with PropertyValue unwrapping, a new time generic, and Flow Strict with exact types.

Contributing: Generated files index.d.ts and index.js.flow must never be edited directly, and contributors must run git config merge.ours.driver true after forking to prevent rebase conflicts. All typings changes originate from generator sources and are committed to make diffs reviewable.

{"memo": "CSSType: CSSType provides TypeScript and Flow type definitions for CSS generated from MDN data to enable autocompletion and static checking of properties and values. Usage is illustrated with TypeScript and Flow imports where misspelled properties or invalid values produce type errors.

Getting started: Installation is done with a single npm install command for the csstype package. No further setup is required to start importing the types in a project.

Table of content: The table lists the main documentation sections to aid navigation. It links to style and rule and usage and troubleshooting and version and contribution topics.

Style types: Properties are grouped by category: All, Standard, Vendor, Obsolete, and Svg, with Standard/Vendor split into Longhand/Shorthand subcategories. Four variations exist: Default camelCase, Hyphen kebab-case, Fallback allowing value arrays, and HyphenFallback combining both.

At-rule types: At-rule types model descriptors for counter style and font face and viewport rules in dedicated interfaces with Default and Hyphen and Fallback variations. In TypeScript they are accessed through the AtRule namespace while in Flow they use an AtRule dollar prefix.

Pseudo types: Pseudo types provide string literals for pseudo classes and pseudo elements under the Pseudos type. Pseudos extends AdvancedPseudos for function like pseudos that need arguments and SimplePseudos for plain single variation pseudos.

Generics: All interfaces accept two optional generics that control allowed length and time value types for greater flexibility. Length defaults to string or zero since zero needs no unit and time defaults to string, and both can be widened to accept numbers for platforms that handle units automatically.

Usage: Basic usage imports the types and assigns plain objects to Properties for standard checking of values like width and margin. Extended patterns support fallback arrays for CSS in JS, literal pseudo selectors, hyphen cased properties by extension, and assignment onto HTMLElement style objects.

What should I do when I get type errors?: Type errors are addressed by first verifying correct CSS usage and checking for rejected specs or widening issues, then searching existing issues and filing a new one if needed. Local fixes use module augmentation or type assertion in TypeScript and type assertion in Flow, including patterns for missing properties and custom properties.

Version 3.2: This release breaks compatibility with version two so both major versions cannot coexist without conflicts. The documented remedy is to force resolution to the newer major line with an overrides entry in package JSON.

Version 3.1: This release exposes shared data types for reuse across projects. TypeScript accesses them through the DataType namespace while Flow uses a DataType dollar prefix.

Version 3.0: This major release moves all property and at rule types into dedicated namespaces and withdraws direct exposure of data types that may change. It also adds a string intersection hack for better autocompletion with an unpack helper plus a new time generic and stricter exact Flow types.

Contributing: Contributions must never edit the generated definition files directly since they are produced automatically and committed for change tracking. Contributors should enable the ours merge driver after cloning and use the provided npm scripts for building and watching and testing and full validation.

Commands: The commands support generating typings with type checking and rebuilding on save. Additional scripts run tests and perform combined type checking with linting and formatting.

Recommendation: For the library selection decision, csstype is recommended as a lightweight, well-maintained source of truth for CSS in TypeScript and Flow that improves correctness and developer experience without runtime cost, subject to standardizing on major version 3 and documenting local workarounds for custom properties and version conflicts.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Inserted W1 Style types summary into W2 document-order sections to achieve full coverage, preserved each worker wording as one paragraph per section, and added closing recommendation per brief."}

{"memo": "Executive Summary: csstype — Library Selection Memo for Architecture Council

CSSType: CSSType provides TypeScript and Flow type definitions for CSS generated from MDN data to enable autocompletion and type checking for properties and values. It is imported as a type namespace and flags misspelled properties or invalid values at compile time.

Getting started: Installation is done with a single npm install command for csstype. No further configuration is required to begin importing its types.

Table of content: The table of content lists the major documentation sections for style types and at-rule types and pseudo types and generics and usage and troubleshooting and version history and contributing. It serves as navigation to quickly locate reference material in the document.

Style types: Properties split into All, Standard (with Longhand/Shorthand), Vendor (Longhand/Shorthand), Obsolete, and Svg categories across Default (camelCase), Hyphen (kebab-case), Fallback (array values), and HyphenFallback variations (e.g., Properties, PropertiesHyphenFallback).

At-rule types: At-rule types describe descriptors for counter-style and font-face and viewport rules through naming variations for default and hyphen and fallback forms. In TypeScript they live under the AtRule namespace while in Flow they use an AtRule prefix.

Pseudo types: Pseudo types provide string literals for pseudo classes and pseudo elements under the Pseudos type. They distinguish AdvancedPseudos for function-like cases requiring arguments from SimplePseudos for plain single-variation cases.

Generics: All interfaces accept optional generics for length defaulting to string or zero since zero needs no unit and time defaulting to string. Callers can widen these generics to numeric types so platforms that interpret numbers with fixed units type check correctly.

Usage: Basic usage imports the namespace and assigns plain objects to Properties for standard checking of values like width and margin. Fallback arrays and hyphen-cased interfaces and pseudo-mapped objects and direct assignment to element styles extend the same pattern for broader scenarios.

What should I do when I get type errors?: When type errors appear the guide advises first verifying correct CSS usage and awareness of widening and unaccepted specs then searching or filing issues. It then shows how to fix problems locally with module augmentation or type assertion in TypeScript and type assertion in Flow including support for custom properties.

Version 3.2: Version 3.2 is no longer compatible with version 2 and conflicts may occur if both are installed. The guide recommends forcing a single resolution with an npm overrides entry for csstype.

Version 3.1: Version 3.1 exposes shared CSS data types for direct reuse. These types are reachable through dedicated namespaces in both TypeScript and Flow.

Version 3.0: Version 3.0 moves all property and at-rule types under dedicated namespaces while withholding unstable data types. It also introduces autocompletion helpers with unpacking utilities plus a new time generic and stricter exact Flow types.

Contributing: Contributing prohibits direct edits to generated definition files since they are produced automatically and committed for change tracking. Contributors must set the recommended git merge driver after cloning to prevent rebase conflicts.

Commands: The commands section defines npm scripts for building and watching and testing the typings. It also provides a lazy script that combines type checking with linting and formatting.

Recommendation: Recommend adoption of csstype for any TypeScript/Flow CSS-in-JS or style-object work: it is zero-runtime, install-trivial, MDN-grounded, and provides broad property, at-rule, pseudo, fallback, and generic coverage with clear troubleshooting and extensibility paths; ensure a single v3.x resolution via overrides to avoid v2 conflicts.", "concerns": ["Memo assembled solely from W1 and W2 summaries without independent read of README; fidelity depends on their accuracy"], "rationale": "Assembled W2 two-sentence summaries and W1 Style types summary in inferred document order (CSSType through Commands) as one paragraph per section plus closing adoption recommendation."}

{"memo": "Executive Summary – csstype Library Selection Memo

CSSType: CSSType provides TypeScript and Flow type definitions for CSS generated from MDN data to enable autocompletion and type checking for properties and values. It is imported as a type namespace in both languages with examples shown for catching misspelled properties and invalid values.

Getting Started: Installation is done with a single package manager command to add csstype as a dependency. No further configuration is required to start importing its types in a project.

Table of Content: The table of content lists the main documentation sections for style types and at-rule types and pseudo types and generics and usage and troubleshooting and version history and contributing. It serves as navigation links to each part of the document.

Style Types: Style types offer CSS property interfaces in five categories—All, Standard, Vendor, Obsolete, Svg—each with four variations: Default (camelCase), Hyphen (kebab-case), Fallback (array values), and HyphenFallback. All combines all categories; Standard and Vendor split into Longhand/Shorthand subcategories.

At-Rule Types: At-rule types provide typed interfaces with descriptors for counter style and font face and viewport rules in matching default and hyphen and fallback variations. They are accessed through the AtRule namespace in TypeScript and through the AtRule dollar prefix in Flow.

Pseudo Types: Pseudo types supply string literals for pseudo classes and pseudo elements grouped under the Pseudos type. Pseudos extends AdvancedPseudos for function-like pseudos that need arguments and SimplePseudos for plain single-variation pseudos.

Generics: All property interfaces accept two optional generics for length and time with length defaulting to string or zero and time defaulting to string. These generics can be widened to string or number to support platforms where numeric lengths or times imply specific units.

Usage: Usage centers on typing style objects with Properties for standard camel cased properties and using PropertiesFallback to allow arrays for fallback values in CSS in JS libraries. It also shows typing pseudo selectors with SimplePseudos and supporting kebab cased names by extending hyphen interfaces and assigning typed objects to element styles.

What Should I Do When I Get Type Errors?: Troubleshooting acknowledges that type errors can stem from user mistakes or evolving specs and vendor implementations despite aiming for perfect types. It advises verifying correctness and checking existing issues then fixing locally with module augmentation or type assertion in TypeScript and type assertion in Flow including support for custom properties.

Version 3.2: This release is no longer compatible with version 2 and conflicts may occur when both major versions are installed together. It recommends forcing resolution to the newer major line through the overrides field in package dot json.

Version 3.1: This release exposes data types through the DataType namespace in TypeScript and the DataType dollar prefix in Flow. It makes reusable value types such as color directly available to consumers.

Version 3.0: This major release moves all property types and at-rule types into dedicated namespaces and stops exposing data types that could be renamed or removed. It also introduces a string and object hack for autocompletion with a helper to unpack values plus a new time generic and Flow strict and exact type improvements.

Contributing: Contributing warns never to edit generated definition files directly since they are produced automatically and committed for change tracking. It requires setting the merge driver to preserve generated files after forking and cloning.

Commands: Commands lists four npm scripts for generating and checking typings and watching for changes and running tests and linting and formatting. They cover build and watch and test and lazy workflows for contributors.

Recommendation: Recommend adoption of csstype for any TypeScript or Flow CSS-in-JS work: it provides comprehensive, MDN-based type safety with flexible handling of vendor, fallback, hyphen, pseudo, at-rule, and generic cases, straightforward installation and usage, and clear guidance for troubleshooting and version migration, with active generated-file maintenance for contributors.", "concerns": [], "rationale": "Assembled memo in document order using W2 two-sentence summaries for all sections except Style types and W1 summary for Style types, adding only a closing synthesis recommendation per assignment."}
